messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Figures: People in uniform, Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Carry Weapon: carry weapon, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Roberto Vázquez

Roberto Vázquez was sixty-three years old when the bomb went off outside the government building in San Salvador where he had gone to renew his residency documentation. He had lived in the United States for thirty-seven years by then, built a successful dental practice in northern California, raised two children, and buried a wife of forty-two years just eighteen months earlier. He had gone back to El Salvador for three weeks to settle some property matters and to visit his aging mother. It was meant to be routine.

He was standing in the hallway outside the administrative office on the second floor, holding a numbered ticket, when the explosion tore through the lobby below. The blast lifted him off his feet. His ears filled with a sound he has never been able to fully describe—not just loud, but something that seemed to unmake the world itself. He fell hard against a concrete wall, his left arm pinned beneath him. For what he thinks was seconds but might have been longer, he lay there unable to move, unable to hear anything but a high-pitched ringing, surrounded by dust so thick he could not see his own hands. When he finally staggered to his feet, he saw blood on the floor—some of it his own from a gash on his forehead, some belonging to people he did not know. Seventeen people died in that attack. He was one of the fortunate ones, his daughter would later tell him.

But fortune is a relative thing. In the weeks after he returned to California, Roberto found himself unable to settle back into the rhythms of his life. He had come to believe that he should have seen it coming, that there had been some warning he had missed, some sign that would have told him not to go to that building on that particular morning. He replayed the morning obsessively—the breakfast he had eaten, the taxi driver's route, the conversation he had had with his mother about whether the trip was necessary. If only he had listened to her hesitation. If only he had waited another day. The self-recrimination became a constant companion, a way of trying to impose order on chaos, as though sufficient blame directed at himself might somehow retroactively prevent what had already happened.

Within months, the world had become a place of constant threat. Any loud noise—a car backfiring, a door slamming in his office building, even the high-pitched whine of his dental drill—sent him into a state of acute vigilance that could take hours to settle. He began carrying a small pistol in his jacket pocket, something he had never done before, telling himself that he needed to be prepared, that he could not afford to be caught unaware again. When he entered his dental office each morning, he would scan the room methodically, noting where the exits were, calculating which route would be fastest if he needed to leave. His hygienist noticed that he had started watching her more carefully, his eyes tracking her movements when she was in the treatment room with him. He could not explain to her why he needed to know where she was at all times, why the sight of her moving toward the supply cabinet made his shoulders tense.

He stopped watching the news. Any report of a bombing, any mention of violence, any footage of uniformed police or military personnel sent him into a state of emotional flooding so complete that he had to leave the room. His daughter, concerned about his isolation, had tried to talk with him about what happened, but when she began speaking about it, something in his chest would tighten and the memory would return not as words but as sensation—the pressure of the blast, the taste of dust, the smell of smoke and something else he could not name. It was all there at once, overwhelming him so thoroughly that he could only ask her to stop, to leave him alone.

At seventy, Roberto sits in his dental office—a place he has loved for decades—and feels like a stranger in his own life. His patients have begun to notice his distance, his reluctance to engage in the casual conversation that once came easily. He is considering retirement, though the thought of it terrifies him more than the thought of staying. What brings him to seek help now is his daughter's ultimatum, delivered with love but with firmness: get help, or she will have to step back from their relationship. He is afraid of what talking about it might do to him, but he is more afraid of losing what little remains of his connection to the people he loves.
